Learning goals
By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:
explain the time-frequency resolution tradeoff in an STFT;
compute the scale and translation of a mother wavelet;

distinguish continuous wavelet analysis from a discrete multiresolution
decomposition; and

interpret two-dimensional Fourier and wavelet coefficients in image
processing.
Gabor transform
Problem:
Although the Fourier transform provides detailed information about the frequency content of a given signal, it does not give any information about when in time those frequencies occur.
For a signal with non-stationary frequency content, such as a musical composition, it is important to simultaneously characterize the frequency content and its evolution in time.
The [Gabor transform]{style=“color: blue”}, aka the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), computes a windowed FFT in a moving window.
This STFT enables the localization of frequency content in time, resulting in the [spectrogram]{style=“color: blue”}, which is a plot of frequency versus time.
What the original figure plots.
It shows signal with frequency content that changes over time.
What this is trying to convey.
A global Fourier spectrum shows which frequencies occur but not when they occur.

Wavelets exploit a multiresolution decomposition that provides different time
and frequency resolutions in different frequency bands.

2D wavelet image compression
Similar to the FFT, the discrete wavelet transform is extensively used for image processing and compression.
In the figure below, the hierarchical nature of the wavelet decomposition is seen.
The upper left corner of the DWT image is a low-resolution version of the image, and the subsequent features add fine details to the image.

What this is trying to convey.
The upper-left approximation and horizontal, vertical, and diagonal detail subbands form a multiresolution representation.

2D wavelet image compression (continued)
The hierarchical representation of data in the wavelet transform is ideal for image compression.
Even with an aggressive truncation, retaining only 0.5

children.html: %\%%

If the transform concentrates signal energy into relatively few coefficients,
thresholding and encoding those coefficients can yield effective compression.
Which details are preserved depends on the wavelet, coefficient-selection rule,
and distortion metric; the largest coefficients are not universally the
"most important" for every task.

filter.endBefore: ## Construction and Properties of Haar or Daubechies Wavelets

children.value: Motivation {#motivation-4 .unnumbered}

The CWT provides a time-frequency representation of signals, allowing the analysis of signals whose frequency content changes over time (non-stationary signals). It is superior to standard Fourier analysis in revealing localized spectral features.
Tasks {#tasks-5 .unnumbered}
Select or generate a non-stationary signal (e.g., chirp, amplitude-modulated wave, or speech).
Implement the continuous wavelet transform using a chosen mother wavelet (e.g., Morlet or Mexican Hat).
Compute and plot the scalogram (magnitude of CWT coefficients as a function of time and scale).
Compare with short-time Fourier transform (STFT) analysis of the same signal.
Identify features in the signal that are better resolved with wavelets than with STFT.
Investigate how the choice of mother wavelet affects time-frequency resolution.
Hints {#hints-5 .unnumbered}
Normalize time and scale axes appropriately to interpret frequency content.
Use available libraries such as PyWavelets in Python or MATLAB Wavelet Toolbox.
Consider converting wavelet scales to pseudo-frequencies for easier interpretation.
Compare time localization of features between CWT and STFT to illustrate the advantage of wavelets.

filter.startAfter: ## Construction and Properties of Haar or Daubechies Wavelets

children.value: Motivation {#motivation-5 .unnumbered}

Wavelets provide a multi-resolution decomposition of signals, useful for compression, denoising, and analysis. Haar wavelets are the simplest orthogonal wavelets, while Daubechies wavelets offer compact support and vanishing moments.
Tasks {#tasks-6 .unnumbered}
Construct the Haar wavelet scaling function and mother wavelet analytically.
Demonstrate the orthogonality of Haar wavelet basis functions.
Implement a discrete Haar wavelet transform (DWT) for a sample signal or image.
Reconstruct the original signal from the Haar coefficients and compare with the original.
Explore Daubechies wavelets (e.g., D4 or D6):
Generate scaling and wavelet filter coefficients.
Verify orthogonality numerically.
Analyze the vanishing moments.
Apply multi-resolution analysis (MRA) to decompose a signal into coarse and detail components.
Hints {#hints-6 .unnumbered}
Haar wavelet functions are piecewise constant; Daubechies wavelets are compactly supported but not piecewise constant.
Use recursive filter-bank algorithm to implement DWT efficiently.
Check that the reconstruction error is close to zero to verify correctness.
Plot the approximation and detail coefficients at each decomposition level to understand MRA.
